title: Describe, represent, analyse and explain changes in shape and motion in 2- and 3-dimensional space with justification

lessons.title: Shapes, transformations and position in 2D
lessons.html:
Describing shape and position

Maths of shape and space is used every day on a farm or game ranch: reading maps, planning a boma, building a kraal, calculating water in a tank, or understanding how a bullet travels. This unit asks you to describe, represent and analyse changes in shape and motion, and to justify (explain and prove) your answers.

Coordinates and maps

A position on a flat surface can be given by coordinates (x; y) on a grid, or by grid references on a map. A map has a scale. On a 1:50 000 topographical map, 1 cm on the map is 50 000 cm (500 m) on the ground. So 4 cm on the map is 4 × 500 m = 2 000 m = 2 km. Direction is given as a compass bearing in degrees from north: east is 90°, south 180°, west 270°.

Transformations

TransformationWhat changesExample
Translation (slide)Position onlyMoving a feeding trough 5 m east
Reflection (flip)Position and orientation, across a mirror lineTwo halves of a symmetrical gate
Rotation (turn)Orientation around a fixed pointA windmill blade turning around the hub
Enlargement or reductionSize, but not shapeA scale drawing of a shed

Translations, reflections and rotations keep size and shape the same: the shapes are congruent. Enlargements keep shape but change size: the shapes are similar, with all lengths multiplied by the same scale factor. If a pen plan is enlarged by a factor of 3, a 4 m side becomes 12 m, but the area becomes 3 × 3 = 9 times larger.

Symmetry

A shape has line symmetry if a mirror line divides it into two matching halves. Many animal tracks are nearly symmetrical: a buck's cloven hoof print has two halves.

lessons.title: 3D objects, measurement and motion
lessons.html:
Three-dimensional objects

Solids such as cubes, rectangular prisms (boxes), cylinders (water tanks), cones and pyramids can be represented in different ways:

  • Nets: the flat shape that folds to make the solid. A cylinder's net is two circles and a rectangle.
  • Views: the plan (from above), front elevation and side elevation, used in building drawings.
  • Perspective drawings, showing depth.

Surface area and volume

Volume of a rectangular prism = length × breadth × height. A cement water trough 2 m × 0.5 m × 0.4 m holds 0.4 m³ = 400 litres (1 m³ = 1 000 L).

Volume of a cylinder = π × r² × h. A round tank with radius 1.5 m and height 2 m holds π × 1.5 × 1.5 × 2 ≈ 14.14 m³, about 14 140 litres.

Justification: each step is shown, units are converted, and the answer is checked for sense. A tank of about 3 m across and 2 m high holding about 14 000 L is reasonable.

Surface area tells you how much material is needed, for example paint or sheeting. A closed box has 6 faces; add the area of each.

Motion

Objects in motion trace paths. A windmill blade traces a circle. A thrown object or a bullet follows a curved path called a trajectory because gravity pulls it down from the start. A rifle's line of sight is straight, but the bullet's path curves; the scope is set so that the two cross at the zero distance. Beyond it the bullet drops further below the line of sight, which is why long shots need more skill and are often unethical for inexperienced hunters.

Speed = distance ÷ time. A bakkie travelling 30 km in 0.5 hours averages 60 km/h.

Key points

  • Use coordinates, scale and bearings to describe position.
  • Translations, reflections and rotations keep shapes congruent; enlargements make similar shapes.
  • Scaling lengths by k scales area by k × k.
  • Volume of a prism is l × b × h; of a cylinder is π × r² × h; 1 m³ = 1 000 L.
  • Justify answers by showing steps, units and a sense check.
